title: Multi-port memories and register files
summary: Many designs need more than one access per clock: a FIFO writes and reads, a CPU reads two operands and writes one result, two processors share a buffer. This topic covers single-, dual- and multi-port memories, register files with bypass, collisions and dual-clock memories — with their SystemVerilog templates.
objectives: Compare single-port, simple dual-port, true dual-port memories and register files.
Write SDP, TDP and register-file models in SystemVerilog.
Explain write-through bypass and implement it.
Recognise port collisions and check them with an assertion.

blocks.caption: Memory port types

blocks.title: Ports cost area
blocks.md: Every port adds word lines, bit lines and decoders to **every** cell. A two-port SRAM cell has 8 transistors instead of 6; register files with many ports are built from flip-flops. Use the fewest ports that meet the bandwidth.

A second port is not free: every cell must be reachable from both sides. In an SRAM this means a second **word line** and a second pair of **bit lines** per cell (8 transistors instead of 6). In a register file every register feeds **every read multiplexer**.

blocks.caption: What two ports allow

blocks.md: A CPU reads two operands and writes one result every clock — a **2R1W register file**. Reads are usually asynchronous, so a value written in this cycle is only visible next cycle — unless a **bypass** forwards it:

steps.title: Without bypass
steps.md: Register 5 is written and read in the same cycle. The write happens at the clock edge, so the read still sees the old value 10.

steps.title: With bypass
steps.md: A comparator sees that the read address equals the write address and forwards the new data 99 directly.

blocks.caption: Write + write to one address: undefined. Write + read: old, new or X, depending on the memory

blocks.md: When two ports access the **same address** in the same cycle, the result depends on the memory:

rows: write A and write B, same address
write A, read B, same address
old data, new data, or X — see the datasheet / tool
read A and read B, same address
both get the same data — no problem
blocks.caption: Same-address access on two ports

blocks.md: A true dual-port or simple dual-port RAM with **different clocks** on its ports is the core of an **asynchronous FIFO**: one clock domain writes, the other reads. The memory itself is safe; the difficulty is passing the read and write **pointers** between the domains — solved with Gray-code counters and synchronisers in the *Designing with Memories* training.

blocks.title: A detail experts check
blocks.md: The SystemVerilog standard forbids writing one variable from two `always_ff` blocks. FPGA synthesis tools recognise the template above with `always`; some also accept a single array written from two `always_ff` blocks with a warning. Follow the template of your tool.
**Collision check** — an assertion that flags two writes to the same address (both ports on one clock):

blocks.title: Different clocks
blocks.md: With two clocks, "same cycle" has no exact meaning — collisions are avoided by the protocol, for example by a FIFO's full/empty logic.
